title: From Freight Yard to Shared Space
text:
For most of the twentieth century, the East Junction freight yard sat behind a row of warehouses near the center of Bellhaven. Trains once delivered coal, machine parts, and produce there, but freight traffic declined after new highway routes opened outside the city. By the late 1990s, several tracks had been removed, two storage buildings were empty, and a large paved area was used mainly for temporary parking. The city bought the property in 2018 after residents and neighborhood groups argued that the abandoned yard divided two growing parts of Bellhaven and blocked safe walking routes between them. Officials said the site could become public space, but they also warned that old industrial land sometimes requires expensive environmental cleanup before redevelopment can begin.

The first planning proposal called for replacing most of the freight-yard structures with a park, apartment buildings, and a wide pedestrian path. Preservation groups objected to removing the brick dispatch office and the steel loading canopy, arguing that the surviving structures were evidence of the city's industrial history. Nearby residents supported better access across the property but disagreed about how much new housing should be added. Some wanted more apartments near the transit station, while others worried that taller buildings would increase traffic on narrow local streets. Instead of approving the first proposal, the city created a public design committee and asked it to review historical records, traffic studies, soil tests, and comments from residents.

The committee eventually recommended a compromise. The dispatch office would be repaired and converted into a small community room, and the loading canopy would remain as a covered market space. A new walking and cycling route would cross the site from east to west, while two apartment buildings would be placed near the existing transit station rather than along the residential edge. The plan also reserved part of the former parking area for trees and a rain garden designed to collect storm water. Before construction could begin, however, soil testing found petroleum contamination near an area where fuel had once been stored. Cleanup added nearly eight months to the schedule and required the city to remove contaminated soil and monitor groundwater.

When the first phase opened in 2024, the cross-site path immediately became the most heavily used part of the project. City counts showed that hundreds of people used it on weekdays to reach buses, shops, and schools without walking around the old freight-yard fence. Weekend markets under the preserved canopy also attracted vendors from nearby neighborhoods. The apartment buildings were still under construction, and the community room could open only on limited days because the city had not yet hired permanent staff for it. Supporters said the project had already reconnected neighborhoods while keeping visible pieces of local history. Critics responded that the delayed housing and limited community-room hours showed that the redevelopment was not yet delivering all of the benefits promised during planning.

Bellhaven officials now describe East Junction as a long-term redevelopment rather than a finished park project. The city plans to review pedestrian counts, market use, traffic, housing occupancy, and maintenance costs after all phases are open. Officials have not promised that every feature will remain unchanged. They say future adjustments may be needed if traffic patterns, operating costs, or public use differ from the planning estimates.
